newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FOCUS - Ukraine economic plan to kickstart output.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Ukraine economic plan to kickstart output.

text.p: The Ukrainian government's economic plan for 1997, described by ministers as the toughest ever, aims to kick start the production sector still in decline five years after independence.

"The priority of the new programme devised by the government is to find ways to help the production sector survive," President Leonid Kuchma told reporters on Thursday during a tour of southern Ukraine.
The plan, unveiled by Economy Minister Vasyl Hureyev, is to be presented to parliament in accordance with Ukraine's first post-Soviet constitution passed in June.

Figures based on the 1997 draft budget submitted to the assembly last week, foresaw the first economic growth since the fall of Communism at 1.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP). GDP fell 8.7 percent in the first two quarters of this year, while last year it plunged 11.8 percent.
Ministers have pledged to keep to a proposed budget deficit of two percent of GDP by Western calculations and in implementing bankruptcy laws that will shut down chronically loss-making factories.
They aim to halve inflation to an annual rate of 24.9 percent, against a forecast 48 percent this year.

"This programme is more concrete and tougher than any other produced by the government. It sets down what state bodies will do to achieve growth in the economy and move on with economic reforms," Hureyev said.
"Honestly, when I read this document I am filled with horror as to how we are to fulfill this. But it will be done."

President Leonid Kuchma has long been under pressure from a big industrial lobby to help industry get back on its feet. And Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko has advocated protectionist measures to boost domestic production.
Hundreds of factories remain idle and markets are flooded with cheap consumer items from Turkey, Poland and developing countries.
A payments crisis has left millions of workers unpaid for months, despite repeated assurances to clear wage arrears worth $1.5 billion.
Ukraine has been under pressure to cut the budget deficit since the International Monetary Fund (IMF) suspended credits early in the year after Kiev overshot its spending targets.

The IMF this week agreed to extend the latest instalment of a $867 million standby credit arrangment. Discussions are under way ove a $2.5 to $3 billion extended fund facility -- a sign that the country's economic health is on the mend.
Hureyev said the government wanted to bring under control Ukraine's shadow economy, estimated to account for 40 percent of economic activity.
Ministers say that could mean declaring an amnesty for anyone who has illegally taken money out of the former Soviet republic -- a sum probably totalling several billion dollars.
"We will just have to tell them: 'Boys, just bring the money back and nothing will happen to you,'" Kuchma told local officials in southern Ukraine.
The programme also called for new action on Ukraine's privatisation programme, which is gradually gaining momentum after a sluggish start.
Hureyev said the government hoped to complete the programme of certificates launched this year and move into "real" money privatisation targeting large factories.
